reviews.one_line_contribution: That cross-model agent-memory harm is signed in the writer-to-reader capability gap (downward transfer hurts, upward does not) rather than a symmetric identity mismatch, that the cure is reader-in-the-loop selection rather than reader authorship, and that coupling a GEPA-style optimizer to the memory bank absorbs the harm in net accuracy while the break-count asymmetry survives underneath.
reviews.closest_prior_work: Agent Memory Distillation (arXiv:2608.07169), as the proposal itself concedes: it already reports that teacher-to-student memory transfer yields inconsistent or degrading results and that quality depends on teacher-student compatibility. That is the phenomenon plus a compatibility term, i.e. most of the qualitative content of Prediction 1. Rosetta Memory (2606.07711) collides on the framing that utility depends on the write/read model pair. What is left after both is narrow: making compatibility ordinal and signed, the quality/utility rank inversion, and the selection-vs-authorship split. Run D is the single cell that separates this proposal from Rosetta/MemCollab, and it is exactly the cell the plan runs at one bank replicate and labels directional only, so the discriminating evidence for the paper's headline framing is the weakest evidence in the design.
reviews.strongest_objection: Prediction 1's direction asymmetry is confounded with reader identity, and no arm controls for it. The difference-in-differences compares (8B reading the 14B bank minus 8B reading its own) against (14B reading the 8B bank minus 14B reading its own): the two arms of the DiD use different readers, so the well-known fact that larger models are less perturbed by any injected prompt text - irrelevant, scrambled, or merely off-policy - predicts the same signed asymmetry with no writer-to-reader capability law at all. Run L cannot break the tie because both its policies sit at the same capability level, and the shuffled-provenance placebo only tests bookkeeping, not reader sensitivity. Add to this that runs D, E, H, I, J, K are single-replicate and self-declared directional only, while Predictions 1 (mirror cell), 4 and 5 all rest on them, in a setting where the track's own pilot saw 5-14 point re-scoring drift. Prediction 5 compounds this by treating a failure to reject (H vs I falling below a 4-5 point MDE) as positive evidence of masking - that is accepting the null, on an underpowered single-replicate contrast, for one of the four claims the proposal says are its remaining novelty. Prediction 4b is separately broken as stated: GEPA (run G) searches 12 candidates scored on reader rollouts while run J is one cold frontier instruction, so candidate count and validation-set exposure differ alongside selection, and 'same author, selection is the only difference' is not true of the arms as designed.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: Four changes, all inside the stated envelope if the n=300 cross-family arm (L) is dropped, since the proposal already concedes L cannot exclude a small stylistic effect. (1) Add a per-reader perturbation calibration: inject token-matched degraded items (scrambled, topically-retrieved-but-wrong, or same-bank items with actions corrupted) into 8B and 14B, and report the provenance effect normalized by each reader's own sensitivity to injected junk; without this the signed-gap law and 'strong readers absorb bad advice' are observationally identical. (2) Promote run D to two bank replicates and enter it in the mixed-effects model as a primary contrast rather than reporting it as directional. (3) Rebuild J as best-of-12 frontier-proposed instructions selected by the frontier model or by a held-out non-reader judge, so G vs J varies only who did the selecting, not how many candidates existed. (4) State Prediction 5 as a pre-registered equivalence test (TOST with a named equivalence margin) rather than 'falls below the MDE', and pre-specify the break-count contrast with an interval, since break counts on the order of 3 vs 6 items cannot support a 2x ratio claim (Prediction 3) at any useful confidence.
reviews.missing_baseline: Reader-probe selection applied to the self-written bank, and a non-reader-selected frontier bank (items filtered by frontier or held-out-model probes at the same admission rate). As designed, run K vs run C shows only that filtering a bank at fixed injected tokens helps - the track's own prior finding that cutting injection from seven items to three removed the harm makes generic filtering the leading rival explanation for the entire Prediction 4a effect. Without a probe-selected self bank (does selection help even when provenance is already matched?) and a non-reader selector (is the benefit reader-specific or just selection-shaped?), the paper's central 'selection, not authorship' claim has no arm that isolates the reader's role in selection. Second omission: a token-matched neutral-filler condition against run A, so that any bank-vs-no-memory statement is not confounded with context length.
reviews.preprint_collision: Unusually good by the standards of this exercise: it names specific arXiv identifiers with dates, dispositions each one, distinguishes collision-on-phenomenon from collision-on-claim, admits AMD is more damaging than a previous read, and states a residual risk. I credit it. Two real weaknesses remain. First, it reports conclusions but no searches: no queries, no venues, no date cutoff, no statement of what was searched and found empty, so 'nothing in the retrieved literature tests any of the four' is unauditable. Second, the search is aimed entirely at the cross-model memory literature and not at the claim the proposal calls its own most novel - that a prompt optimizer masks component-level harm in a coupled optimizer-plus-memory stack. Component-attribution and ablation-hygiene work on DSPy/GEPA-style stacks is the natural place for that to have been scooped, and the check does not report looking there. On the collision that is admitted: AMD's compatibility term plus Rosetta's write/read-pair dependence already occupy the descriptive claim, so the novelty that survives is the sign of the effect - which rides on the single underpowered cell (run D) flagged above - plus the selection/authorship split, whose isolating arms are themselves confounded. The proposal's own residual-risk sentence (a self-written-bank ablation sitting in some cross-model memory appendix) names precisely the finding that would leave only the masking result standing.

reviews.one_line_contribution: Memory-item utility is claimed to fall with the *directed* writer to reader capability gap (frontier-written items hurt an 8B reader while 8B-written items do not hurt a 14B reader), the cure is reader-side *selection* rather than reader *authorship*, and coupling a GEPA-style optimizer to the memory bank hides that harm at net accuracy while it survives in the break-count decomposition.
reviews.closest_prior_work: AMD / Agent Memory Distillation (arXiv:2608.07169, 2026) is the sharpest threat, and the proposal itself concedes why: AMD already reports that teacher-to-student memory 'yields inconsistent improvements and in several cases degrades performance' and that transfer quality 'depends on both teacher accuracy and teacher-student compatibility.' Harm plus a compatibility term is therefore prior. Rosetta Memory (2606.07711) independently formalizes write-model/read-model dependence. What is left to this proposal is a sign on an already-reported compatibility term, a fix/break decomposition, and the masking result -- a refinement, not a new phenomenon. Secondarily, the on-policy distillation line (self-generated data beating teacher-generated data because of distribution mismatch) makes the signed direction the expected outcome rather than a surprising one; the proposal's defense (the training-free regime does not entail it) is fair but makes the prediction low-information if it confirms.
reviews.strongest_objection: Prediction 5, the masking claim -- the most novel thing in the proposal -- is not testable at the stated design. It asks that the H-vs-I (self bank vs frontier bank under GEPA instructions) net-accuracy difference 'falls below the MDE,' i.e. it claims a null. Establishing that an effect has been masked requires showing the H-I difference is *smaller* than the B-C difference, an interaction whose variance is roughly sqrt(2) that of a single contrast, giving an MDE of ~6 points by the proposal's own arithmetic -- while the base effect it is supposed to shrink is predicted at only 4 points. The shrinkage the paper wants to report is therefore undetectable by construction. Worse, H, I, G and J each rest on a *single* GEPA optimization run, and the variance of GEPA's own search is never estimated anywhere: run M re-seeds decoding only, not optimization. The proposal's own Measurement section reports pilot drift of 5-14 points and a treatment-free replicate that mimicked the best real treatment; a single-seed prompt-search difference is exactly the kind of quantity that noise floor swallows. The identical arithmetic sinks the primary asymmetry claim: run D's mirror cell (14B reads 8B bank) carries only one bank replicate, so by the proposal's own rule it is 'directional only,' yet prediction 1's difference-in-differences -- the sole contrast that discriminates the signed account from Rosetta/MemCollab's symmetric one -- is computed from it. The cells that decide the paper are the ones run at the lowest power tier.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: Reallocate episodes from the cells that the proposal already admits are uninformative to the cells that decide the claims. Drop run L outright -- the proposal concedes n=300 gives MDE 6-7 points and that it 'will not read a sub-6-point null there as evidence of parity,' so it cannot exclude a stylistic-affinity effect of the same size as the primary effect and buys nothing -- and spend those four runs on (a) a second bank replicate for both run D direction cells, so the primary difference-in-differences carries estimable bank variance, and (b) a second independent GEPA optimization seed for G/H/I/J, so the masking difference can be separated from prompt-search variance. Restate prediction 5 as a prespecified interaction (or a TOST equivalence test with a stated margin, e.g. the H-I difference is bounded within +/-2 points while B-C exceeds 4), never as 'falls below the MDE.' Add the two missing controls on run K (below). Finally, add a paraphrase arm -- the 8B rewrites frontier items verbatim in content but in its own idiom -- to separate 'the advice names actions beyond the reader's competence' from 'the surface form is off-distribution'; without it, the executability readout in prediction 7 is consistent with both, and only the first supports the capability-gap framing.
reviews.missing_baseline: Run K has no controls of its own, and it carries the mechanism claim. Two are needed. (1) Reader-probe selection applied to the *self* bank. If probe filtering lifts the self bank by as much as it lifts the frontier bank, 'selection, not authorship' collapses into 'filtering helps any bank,' and prediction 4(a) becomes uninterpretable. (2) A random-subset frontier bank matched to K's *surviving item count*, not merely to its injected token budget. K keeps only items that survive three probe replays and then pads to the token budget -- padding equalizes tokens but not the number of distinct actionable recommendations, and the track's own starting position is that injection volume (seven items to three), not content, was the causal lever that eliminated harm. As written, K's predicted 50% recovery is fully explained by the already-known volume effect, and the proposal never rules it out. A third omission: no arm has the 8B *author* a bank from the 14B's traces, the mirror of run E; without it, 'who acted' and 'who wrote' are decomposed in only one direction.
reviews.preprint_collision: Well above the norm and it should be credited as such: it names specific arXiv identifiers, concedes that AMD already reports both the harm and a compatibility term, states plainly that 'the novelty of cross-model agent memory transfers badly is gone as of mid-2026,' names the residual risk (a self-written-bank ablation in some appendix), and reports an OpenReview check. I found no preprint that makes the masking claim. But the check searches for collisions on the phenomenon it has already surrendered, not on the claims it is defending. Nothing is searched for reader-verified or rollout-gated memory admission -- success-gated and validated-insight writing is already routine practice in the ExpeL/ReasoningBank line, so 'reader-in-the-loop selection helps' is close to a described technique and the genuinely new part is only the selection-vs-authorship *contrast*; nothing is searched for optimizer-memory interaction or attribution in coupled systems, which is where the paper's freshest claim lives. No search queries, dates, or venue scope are given. So: an honest, unusually specific check that is nonetheless aimed at the wrong target, and it leaves the two surviving contributions unverified.

reviews.one_line_contribution: That cross-model agent-memory harm is not symmetric identity mismatch but a *signed* writer→reader capability effect, that the fix is reader-in-the-loop selection rather than reader authorship (shown in both the memory and instruction slots), and that coupling a GEPA-style optimizer to a memory bank masks the residual harm at the net-accuracy level while the break asymmetry survives underneath.
reviews.closest_prior_work: Rosetta Memory (arXiv:2606.07711) and AMD (arXiv:2608.07169). AMD already reports that teacher→student memory transfer 'yields inconsistent improvements and in several cases degrades performance' and that quality depends on 'teacher–student compatibility' — so both the harm and a compatibility term are prior, and the proposal concedes this. Rosetta threatens the framing, and the proposal's escape hatch is weaker than it claims: it asserts that identity/style accounts are 'symmetric' and therefore falsified by run D. That is a straw version of the rival. A style/brittleness account predicts asymmetry too, because a weaker reader is more perturbable by *any* off-distribution phrasing than a stronger one is; harm falling harder on the 8B is exactly what Rosetta's mechanism would produce without any ordinal capability law. So the single cell that is supposed to separate this proposal from its closest competitor does not separate them.
reviews.strongest_objection: The two headline claims rest on cells that are both underpowered and, by the proposal's own accounting, non-primary. (a) Run D — the direction-asymmetry cell, explicitly billed as 'the discriminating test' against Rosetta/MemCollab — is 2 runs with a single bank replicate, and Measurement §(b) says non-primary single-replicate cells are 'reported as directional only'. Its DiD MDE is ~6 points and prediction 1 asks for exactly ≥6: any positive is at the detection edge, and the mirror leg is stated as 'no penalty of comparable size', i.e. accepting a null in the cell with the *largest* variance in the design. The proposal itself refuses to read a sub-6 null as parity for run L; prediction 1 does precisely that for run D. (b) Prediction 5, the masking result, is defined as H−I 'falling below the MDE' — again a null, again in single-replicate cells (H and I are 2 runs each, one per reader), against a noise floor the proposal admits produced 5–14 point drift and a treatment-free replicate that mimicked the best real treatment. A shrinking net delta under GEPA is equally explained by GEPA raising accuracy toward ceiling, by GEPA reducing discordant-pair rate (and hence power), or by the single replicate. As written, the most novel claim in the paper is an underpowered null dressed as a mechanism.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: 1) Reallocate bank replicates: run D and the H/I masking pair need two replicates each, more than run E or L do. 2) Replace every 'falls below the MDE' with a preregistered equivalence test (TOST) against a stated equivalence margin, and report the GEPA-condition discordant-pair rate so a power loss cannot be sold as masking. 3) Add a mismatch-without-capability-gap arm: have the frontier rewrite the 8B's *own* items in frontier style/abstraction without adding content, and read it with the 8B. If that arm harms as much as the frontier-authored bank, the effect is style brittleness and the signed-gap law is dead — run E (frontier writing from 8B traces) is the closest thing to this but is a single unreplicated run with no prediction attached to it, so it currently carries no inferential weight. 4) Fix the replicate construction: splitting the 150–250-item intersection into disjoint halves means the primary contrasts are run on 75–125-item banks, so retrieval hit-rate differs from the precheck and from run F; use bootstrap or overlapping resamples at full bank size, or report bank size as a covariate. 5) State what the token 'padding' in runs C and K actually contains — padding is itself a treatment that may differentially load the small reader's context, and it is doing load-bearing work in the one arm (K) that supports the selection claim.
reviews.missing_baseline: A quality-agnostic subsetting control for run K. The track's own established result is that injection *volume* is the causal lever (7 items → 3 items eliminated the harm from the identical bank). Reader-probe admission removes items; padding restores tokens but not distinct advice. So K vs C confounds 'reader selected' with 'fewer distinct items', and prediction 4(a) can be satisfied by volume alone. Required: (i) random-subset frontier bank matched to K's retained item count, (ii) judge-quality-top-k frontier bank at the same count (selection by a non-reader criterion), and (iii) probe selection performed with the *other* reader's probes — only (iii) shows selection must be reader-specific rather than merely a filter. The same hole exists in the instruction slot: G vs J is not 'same author, selection is the only difference' — GEPA also gets 12 candidates and iterative reflection on rollout traces, while J is one cold instruction. The demanded control is frontier-authored best-of-12 selected by the frontier (or by the other reader's rollouts), not a single cold write.
reviews.preprint_collision: Among the better collision checks I have seen on the memory side: it names three colliding 2026 preprints with IDs, quotes AMD against its own interest, concedes that 'cross-model agent memory transfers badly' is no longer novel, dispositions five further papers, and states a residual risk. I credit it and it materially raises my confidence in the positioning. Two gaps keep it from being clean. First, it searched only the memory literature. The most novel claim in the proposal — that a prompt optimizer absorbs and hides a coupled component's harm — has no search behind it at all: no query for GEPA/MIPRO + memory coupling, component attribution, or optimizer-masking preprints, and the cited Cross-Component Interference paper (2605.05716) is the obvious neighbourhood where a masking result could already sit. Second, 'No matching OpenReview submission was found' names no venue, cycle, or date, and given three concurrent cross-model memory preprints it is quite likely that at least one already runs both transfer directions in an evaluation matrix without calling it signed — which would reduce the asymmetry claim from a new law to a reframing of an existing table. The proposal anticipates this only for a 'self-written-bank ablation in an appendix'.
